The Ellsworth Water District published its annual maintenance summary on Tuesday, describing twelve months of repairs across a network that serves roughly forty thousand households. The report opens at the three storage reservoirs, where crews replaced two intake screens and resealed the vault doors that had leaked through the previous winter. According to the summary, the north reservoir lost about nine percent of its capacity to sediment, a figure the engineers call normal for a basin of that age.

Work on the distribution mains accounted for the largest share of the budget. Crews replaced just under six kilometres of cast-iron pipe, most of it laid in the 1930s, and installed new isolation valves at thirty-one intersections. Two of the replacements were unplanned: a section of main beneath Market Street failed in April, flooding three basements, and a joint on the eastern trunk line cracked during a pressure test in August. Both repairs finished inside the district's target window, though the Market Street job ran eleven days over schedule because the contractor had to reroute a gas line.

A series of thunderstorms in late June brought down trees on four feeder roads and tripped a pump station at the western edge of the service area. The summary describes how the emergency crew restored pressure in fourteen hours, and how a mutual-aid agreement with the neighbouring town supplied two generators while the station's own unit was under repair. Shortly after the June storms, the board approved a reserve fund for backup power, a decision the report calls the most significant policy change of the year.

The treatment plant received a new clarifier and a rebuilt chemical feed system. Operators also adjusted the coagulation schedule, which the report credits with a fourteen percent drop in the volume of sludge hauled to the landfill. A short paragraph covers the laboratory, where staff processed more than eighteen thousand samples over the year, including routine checks for bacteria, nitrates and lead at the customer tap.

Customer service drew fewer complaints than in any year since the district began publishing the metric. The billing office attributes the improvement to a new online portal that lets residents track usage by the hour. The report adds that the portal crashed twice during the summer heat wave, and that a temporary call centre absorbed the overflow.

The final section lists the district's plans: a shorter public update in the spring, a lead service line inventory, and the results of the rate study commissioned last autumn. Residents who want a printed copy can request one by calling the office on King Street.
